resources.what_it_is: The canonical text of the technique, serialised as 19 Medium chapters under the "Wardley Maps" publication. It moves from a narrative of strategic failure ("On Being Lost") through the construction of a map, to doctrine, climatic patterns, gameplay, scenario planning and organisational structure. It is deliberately autobiographical — Wardley describes his own failures as CEO of Fotango, the origin of the technique in 2005, and its refinement at Canonical. It is not a textbook; it is a long argument with worked examples, and it is the source every other resource in this list derives from. The full chapter list, verified: 1. On Being Lost — https://medium.com/wardleymaps/on-being-lost-2ef5f05eb1ec 2. Finding a Path — https://medium.com/wardleymaps/finding-a-path-cdb1249078c0 3. Exploring the Map — https://medium.com/wardleymaps/exploring-the-map-ad0266fad59b 4. Doctrine — https://medium.com/wardleymaps/doctrine-8bb0015688e5 5. The Play and a Decision to Act — https://medium.com/wardleymaps/the-play-and-a-decision-to-act-8eb796b1dff1 6. Getting Started Yourself — https://medium.com/wardleymaps/getting-started-yourself-e1a359b785a2 7. Finding a New Purpose — https://medium.com/wardleymaps/finding-a-new-purpose-8c60c9484d3b 8. Keeping the Wolves at Bay — https://medium.com/wardleymaps/keeping-the-wolves-at-bay-93de21b6b2f8 9. Charting the Future — https://medium.com/wardleymaps/anticipation-89692e9b0ced 10. I Wasn't Expecting That! — https://medium.com/wardleymaps/i-wasnt-expecting-that-dcfe122a2234 11. To Thine Own Self Be True — https://medium.com/wardleymaps/to-thine-own-self-be-true-543cfe2cd1a 15. On the Practice of Scenario Planning — https://medium.com/wardleymaps/on-the-practice-of-scenario-planning-49eed8279e90 16. Super Looper — https://medium.com/wardleymaps/round-round-get-around-i-loop-around-d88e865d4337 17. To Infinity and Beyond — https://medium.com/wardleymaps/to-infinity-and-beyond-c7a53ccd2a07 18. Better for Less — https://medium.com/wardleymaps/better-for-less-58fe8c0a3aaa 19. On Playing Chess — https://medium.com/wardleymaps/on-playing-chess-2634b825dbac
resources.limitations: Long (572 pages in the compiled edition), digressive, and structurally uneven. Medium's reading experience is poor for a 19-part work; chapter 9's URL slug ("anticipation") doesn't match its title, which trips up automated indexers. It stops mid-argument — Wardley has said it is unfinished. No index, no glossary, and the diagrams are inline images with no alt text.
resources.attribution: "Wardley Maps by Simon Wardley, licensed CC BY-SA 4.0." Because it is **ShareAlike**, any adapted/derivative content you publish (re-drawn diagrams, restructured chapter summaries) must itself carry CC BY-SA 4.0. Verbatim quotation with attribution is safe; adaptation licence-infects your page.

Active writing has moved to https://swardley.medium.com/ (verified — 15,000 followers, most recent post *"Map Camp … and so it starts"*, 10 June) and to https://www.swardleymaps.com/.

resources.what_it_is: The working notebook where the technique was actually developed in public. It contains the canonical short-form definitions that the book later expanded — most importantly the doctrine list (https://blog.gardeviance.org/2016/08/doctrine.html, 16 August 2016, verified) and the map cheat sheet post (https://blog.gardeviance.org/2016/04/whats-in-wardley-map-and-need-for-cheat.html, verified) which sets out the four constituent parts of a map: **anchor** (user need), **position** (visibility via chain of needs), **types** (activities, practices, data, knowledge), and **evolution** (stages I–IV measured by ubiquity vs certainty, explicitly *not* time-based diffusion). The evolution-axis post (https://blog.gardeviance.org/2014/03/on-mapping-and-evolution-axis.html) is where the ubiquity-vs-certainty derivation is laid out. Also carries much of the polemic that gives Wardley his reputation.
resources.limitations: Blogspot-hosted, poor search, no tagging discipline, images frequently low-resolution. Dormant since Feb 2024 — anything you cite from it is at least 2.5 years stale, and doctrine has since expanded to a 40-principle / 4-phase grid (see Learn Wardley Mapping below) that the blog's 10-item list predates.
resources.attribution: "Simon Wardley, *Bits or pieces?*, CC BY-SA 3.0." ShareAlike applies. Because 3.0 and 4.0 are not identical, keep blog-derived and book-derived material separately attributed rather than merging under one notice.

resources.maintainer: Wikipedia contributors
resources.status: Live, reasonably maintained.
resources.licence: **CC BY-SA 4.0** (Wikipedia standard).
resources.what_it_is: The most useful neutral third-party summary and the best single source for the *history*, which the primary sources scatter. It records that Wardley created the technique at **Fotango in 2005**, building on evolutionary framing developed in 2004, and that **Canonical UK refined it 2008–2010**, with components documented in the 2010 *Better for Less* paper. It states the axes cleanly (Y = value chain position / user visibility; X = evolution: genesis → custom build → product → commodity), notes government adoption (GDS, HS2) and security operations modelling, and — unusually for a Wikipedia article on a management technique — carries a genuine criticism sentence: against Wardley's claim that mapping works by "exposing assumptions, allowing challenge and creating consensus," critics counter it may instead *"launder assumptions into facts, delegitimise challenge (and still create consensus)."*
resources.limitations: Does not cover climatic patterns or gameplay at all. The tools list is stale in places (still lists MapScript and MapKeep). The Simon Wardley biography article is a stub with almost no career detail — do not rely on it for affiliations.
resources.attribution: "Wikipedia contributors, 'Wardley map', CC BY-SA 4.0" with a link back to the article. ShareAlike applies to adaptations.

resources.what_it_is: The de facto second-best entry point after the book, and for most people the *first* one they should actually use. The free half is a structured reference organised the way the technique is actually taught — Purpose, Landscape, Climate, Doctrine, Leadership — plus a glossary, a tools directory, and chapter-by-chapter video summaries of Wardley's book. The doctrine section (https://learnwardleymapping.com/doctrine/ — verified) is the best-rendered version of the full four-phase doctrine grid anywhere: Phase 1 *Stop Self-Destructive Behaviour*, Phase 2 *Becoming More Context Aware*, Phase 3 *Better for Less*, Phase 4 *Continuously Evolving*, with roughly 40 principles distributed across them — substantially more than the 10-item list on Wardley's blog. The paid product is **Pragmatic Wardley Mapping**: 7 modules, 75 minutes of core video plus 298 minutes of bonus material, the Wardley Map Library, and case-study recordings, at **$149 one-time** with lifetime access to current and future iterations and a 30-day money-back guarantee.
resources.limitations: Pricing is a single $149 tier with no cheaper on-ramp, which is a real barrier for individuals. The tools directory, while honest about what's dead, is itself slightly behind (it lists MapKeep as discontinued correctly, but doesn't yet cover Mermaid's `wardley-beta`). Course content is not openly licensed, so you can describe it but not excerpt it.

resources.name: OnlineWardleyMaps (OWM)
resources.url: https://onlinewardleymaps.com/ (verified live — single-page app, so a raw fetch returns only metadata and a loading state; confirmed via meta tags and the docs site). Docs: https://docs.onlinewardleymaps.com/ (verified). Repo: https://github.com/damonsk/onlinewardleymaps (verified).
resources.maintainer: **Damon Skelhorn** (@damonsk). Community handle @MapsAsCode on X/Twitter. Funded via Patreon.
resources.status: **Actively maintained — the healthiest tool in the ecosystem.** 308 stars, 75 forks. Major modernisation released **15 June 2025**: full JavaScript→TypeScript migration, resizable split-pane editor with persisted layout, DSL modernisation replacing legacy `market` and `ecosystem` keywords with unified decorator syntax, memoised React rendering. Stated roadmap: plugin architecture, map analytics, real-time collaborative editing, mobile optimisation.
resources.licence: **MIT** (the code). The mapping technique itself is credited CC BY-SA 4.0 to Simon Wardley.
resources.what_it_is: The reference implementation of maps-as-code, and the de facto standard text format for the entire ecosystem. You type a small DSL in the left pane and a map renders live on the right. The DSL uses `[visibility, maturity]` coordinates on 0–1 scales, where visibility is the Y-axis (0 invisible → 1 visible) and maturity is the X-axis (0 genesis → 1 commodity). Keywords: `component`, `anchor`, `pipeline`, `evolve`, `inertia`, `submap`, `note`, `annotation`, `accelerator`, `deaccelerator`, `title`, `style`, `size`, `url`, `label`; links are `->` (dependency) and `+>` (flow). A minimal example: ``` title Payment System Map component Customer [0.95, 0.2] pipeline Processing [0.5, 0.9] evolve Gateway 0.9 Customer->Website annotation 1 [[0.6, 0.8]] Modernisation needed note Legacy system [0.4, 0.7] ``` The same engine ships as a VS Code extension and an Obsidian plugin, so one syntax covers browser, editor and notes. Architecture is a React front end plus a Node/TypeScript API for save/fetch, with Docker and docker-compose for local running.
resources.limitations: Positioning is manual numeric coordinates — there is no layout engine, so you nudge decimals until it looks right, and large maps become tedious. No real-time multi-user collaboration yet (it is on the roadmap, and MapKeep's death removed the only tool that had it). Being an SPA, maps are not server-side rendered, which hurts sharing and archiving. Single-maintainer bus factor, mitigated only by MIT licensing.
resources.screenshot_target: https://onlinewardleymaps.com/ (the split-pane editor with a map rendered)
resources.attribution: "OnlineWardleyMaps by Damon Skelhorn, MIT licensed. Wardley Mapping provided courtesy of Simon Wardley, CC BY-SA 4.0." MIT permits code reuse with the licence notice; screenshots of the UI are fine with credit.

resources.name: Wardley Maps in Mermaid (`wardley-beta`)
resources.maintainer: Mermaid project (mermaid-js). The Wardley diagram type was contributed by **Mark Craddock** (@tractorjuice), resolving long-standing issue #1661 via **PR #7526** (commit `efe218a`). Craddock's write-up: https://medium.com/learn-wardley-mapping/bringing-wardley-maps-to-mermaid-a-journey-from-idea-to-open-source-contribution-8fe5009eafd3 (verified, published **9 November 2025**).
resources.started: Shipped in **mermaid@11.14.0**. ⚠️ The GitHub releases page rendered the date as "1 April" without a year in my fetch; the surrounding sequence (11.13.0 = 9 March, 11.15.0 = 11 May) and Craddock's November 2025 contribution date imply **April 2026**. Treat the exact release date as approximate and re-verify before publishing.
resources.status: **Live and explicitly beta.** The docs mark it with a 🔥 and the diagram keyword is literally `wardley-beta`. Mermaid 11.15.0 is the current line and the maps still parse under it.
resources.licence: Mermaid is **MIT**.
resources.what_it_is: Native Wardley map rendering inside the world's most widely embedded diagramming library — which means maps now render directly in GitHub markdown, GitLab, Notion, Obsidian, Docusaurus, GitBook and anywhere else Mermaid is supported, with no plugin. The syntax deliberately mirrors OWM: `component Name [visibility, evolution]`, `anchor Name [v, e]`, links `A -> B` (dependency), `A +> B` (flow), `A -.-> B` (dashed), `evolve Name targetEvo`, `note "text" [v, e]`, `annotation N,[x,y] "text"`. Decorators `(inertia)`, `(build)`, `(buy)`, `(outsource)`, `(market)` mark strategic sourcing. It supports custom evolution stages (`evolution Stage1 -> Stage2`), `pipeline Parent { ... }` blocks, and label offsets (`component Name [v, e] label [offsetX, offsetY]`). Critically, coordinates are `[visibility, evolution]` — **not** conventional `[x, y]` — matching OWM and catching out everyone who assumes otherwise. Implementation is a lightweight regex-based parser plus a custom D3 renderer, shipped with 7 unit tests and 12 E2E visual regression tests. Mark Craddock also maintains https://github.com/tractorjuice/wardley-maps-mermaid (verified), a mirror of Simon Wardley's canonical repository with all **147 maps** across 22 domains converted to `wardley-beta`, reporting 100% component/link retention across 4,905 components and 5,172 links, evolution coordinate drift of exactly 0.0, and mean visibility variance of 0.008 — all 147 parse under Mermaid 11.15.0+.
resources.limitations: **Beta, and the keyword says so** — `wardley-beta` will change when it stabilises, so anything you author today may need a keyword rewrite. Handdrawn/rough mode is explicitly unsupported. The regex-based parser is less rigorous than a real grammar and will be less forgiving of edge cases than OWM's. Renderer is bespoke D3, so it does not inherit Mermaid's usual layout machinery. Not all Mermaid *hosts* have upgraded — GitHub, GitLab and others pin older Mermaid versions, so `wardley-beta` may silently fail to render in the exact place you most want it (Joplin, for example, has an open issue just to reach 11.14.0). Verify your host's Mermaid version before promising it works.
resources.attribution: "Mermaid (MIT), Wardley map diagram type contributed by Mark Craddock." Docs prose is subject to Mermaid's licensing — quote briefly with attribution; the syntax itself is not copyrightable.

resources.what_it_is: Renders and edits OWM-format Wardley maps inside Obsidian notes using ` ```wardleymap ` fenced code blocks, supporting components, evolution, annotations and styling. Written in TypeScript. Installed via Settings → Community plugins → Browse → "Wardley Maps".
resources.limitations: No release in ~21 months. AGPL licensing is a genuine consideration for commercial reuse. Small user base (22 stars) means bugs surface slowly. Obsidian-only. **Note:** Obsidian also renders Mermaid natively, so once your Obsidian build ships Mermaid ≥11.14.0, `wardley-beta` code blocks become a plugin-free alternative — check which you actually need.
resources.attribution: "Wardley Maps for Obsidian by Damon Skelhorn, AGPL-3.0."

resources.name: wardleyToGo
resources.maintainer: **Olivier Wulveryck** (@owulveryck)
resources.status: Live. 58 stars. Ships tagged binaries via GitHub Releases.
resources.licence: **MIT**
resources.what_it_is: A Go library plus CLI for treating Wardley maps as data structures rather than pictures. It models maps on a 100×100 coordinate grid of visibility and evolution and renders to SVG. It accepts two input formats: **OnlineWardleyMaps syntax** (so it interoperates with the ecosystem standard) and its own **WTG2 DSL**, which is more expressive — Roman-numeral evolution phases (I–IV) instead of raw decimals, component declarations with coordinates and metadata, edges, annotations (notes, warnings, signals), pipelines, submaps, grouping, custom stages, and block-level configuration for type, colour and notes. The CLI is `wtg2svg`, reading WTG2 on stdin and writing SVG on stdout: `go install github.com/owulveryck/wardleyToGo/cmd/wtg2svg@latest`. A browser playground exists.
resources.limitations: Go-only — no bindings for Python, JS or anything else, which excludes most data-science and web workflows. WTG2 is a second, non-standard DSL that fragments the ecosystem; maps written in it don't open in OWM or Mermaid without conversion. Small community (58 stars), essentially one maintainer. SVG output styling is fixed and less polished than OWM's.
resources.screenshot_target: https://owulveryck.github.io/wardleyToGo/ (the interactive playground) *(unverified — verify before use)*
resources.attribution: "wardleyToGo by Olivier Wulveryck, MIT licensed."

resources.name: cli-owm
resources.maintainer: GitHub user **monkeypants**
resources.started: Newest entry in the awesome list, added around **7 March 2026**.
resources.status: Live but very new and very small — **2 stars**. Treat as promising, unproven.
resources.licence: **MIT**
resources.what_it_is: A Node CLI that renders OnlineWardleyMaps DSL text directly to SVG with no browser involved. It uses the actual OnlineWardleyMaps parser rather than a reimplementation, which is the key design decision — output should stay faithful to the reference renderer. Reads files or stdin, writes files or stdout, ships five built-in visual themes, distributed as an npm package and as standalone binaries. Build with `npm install && npm run build`; the executable lands at `dist/cli.js` and can be `npm link`ed globally.
resources.limitations: 2 stars, no release history verified, single contributor, brand new — do not build a production pipeline on it without pinning a commit. No release/version metadata was visible on the repo page.
resources.attribution: "cli-owm by monkeypants, MIT licensed; uses the OnlineWardleyMaps parser (Damon Skelhorn, MIT)."

resources.name: Map (macOS / Linux) — Tranquil Systems
resources.maintainer: **Rubén Beltrán del Río**, trading as Tranquil Systems (© 2025). Same author as the `wmap-parser-*` family of libraries.
resources.status: **Actively maintained.** Version **4.3.1** current, with a published changelog. macOS (native) and a GTK4 Linux build.
resources.licence: **AGPL-3.0**, source available.
resources.what_it_is: A native desktop Wardley map editor built around the `wmap` text syntax — a *different* DSL from OWM's. Maps are plain text files, so they version-control cleanly, with image export. Being native rather than Electron, it has real macOS integration: Quick Look preview of map files in Finder, iCloud Drive sync for lightweight collaboration, customisable fonts and backgrounds, and smart editing. Completely free — no account, no subscription. It anchors a whole parser/renderer family by the same author: `wmap-parser-js` (npm), `wmap-parser-rust` (crates.io), `wmap-parser-swift`, `wmap-parser-c` (ANSI C), `tree-sitter-wmap` (with a bundled Neovim plugin for syntax highlighting), `wmap-renderer-canvas`, `wmap-renderer-svg`, `wmap-renderer-rust` — plus a fedwiki plugin, `wiki-plugin-wmap`.
resources.limitations: **`wmap` is not the OWM DSL.** This is the single biggest ecosystem fragmentation issue after WTG2: maps authored here do not open in onlinewardleymaps.com, Mermaid, VS Code or Obsidian without conversion. macOS-first with Linux second-class; no Windows, no web. AGPL-3.0 restricts commercial embedding. iCloud "collaboration" is file sync, not real-time co-editing.
resources.attribution: "Map by Rubén Beltrán del Río / Tranquil Systems, AGPL-3.0."

resources.name: ArcKit (Wardley mapping for AI coding assistants)
resources.maintainer: **Mark Craddock** (@tractorjuice) — also the author of Mermaid's Wardley support.
resources.started: Rapid release cadence through 2025–2026; **v5.15.0** current with **1,322 commits**.
resources.status: **Very actively maintained** — 2,000+ stars, 250+ forks.
resources.licence: **MIT**
resources.what_it_is: An enterprise-architecture governance harness for AI coding assistants, with Wardley mapping as a first-class capability rather than an afterthought. It exposes a set of slash commands — `/arckit:wardley` to build a strategic map for component evolution analysis (Genesis → Custom → Product → Commodity), build-vs-buy and vendor comparison, plus specialised variants `wardley.value-chain`, `wardley.doctrine`, `wardley.gameplay` and `wardley.climate` that each drive a different part of the method. It vendors **147 Wardley maps** in-repo as a reference corpus, so the assistant has grounded examples rather than hallucinating from memory. It installs across Claude Code (primary — 13 plugins via marketplace), Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot (`.prompt` files), Mistral Vibe and Codex/OpenCode, and bundles MCP servers for AWS Knowledge, Microsoft Learn and Google Developer Knowledge.
resources.limitations: Wardley mapping is a *feature* of a much larger EA governance product — you take on a great deal of unrelated surface area to get it. Heavily oriented toward UK/enterprise governance concerns (jurisdictional overlays, G-Cloud). Very fast version churn (v0.3 → v5.15 in about a year) means documentation and blog posts go stale quickly. LLM-generated maps inherit all of Matt Edgar's "laundering assumptions into facts" critique, amplified — an agent will confidently place components on the evolution axis with no basis whatsoever.
resources.attribution: "ArcKit by Mark Craddock, MIT licensed." The 147 vendored maps are CC BY-SA 4.0 from Simon Wardley's repository and must be attributed as such separately.

resources.what_it_is: Wardley's signature talk and the best single hour of him explaining the technique. He works through situational awareness and its application to technology strategy: how mapping an environment surfaces opportunities that a spreadsheet or a SWOT cannot, using examples from both UK government and commercial settings. He covers the patterns by which technology evolves, how organisations should restructure around those patterns (pioneers, settlers, town planners), and how leaders can anticipate change rather than react to it. The title is the argument: you cannot plan the crossing in advance, but you can feel for the next stone — provided you have a map that tells you which direction the far bank is in.
resources.limitations: From 2019 — predates the current tooling entirely, and predates his AI-era writing. Multiple near-identical recordings from different conferences create confusion about which is canonical. InfoQ requires no login but does gate some features. Not openly licensed, so no clipping or re-hosting.

resources.name: The map cheat sheet, doctrine list, climatic patterns and gameplay
resources.url: Cheat sheet — https://blog.gardeviance.org/2016/04/whats-in-wardley-map-and-need-for-cheat.html (verified). Doctrine (canonical short list) — https://blog.gardeviance.org/2016/08/doctrine.html (verified). Doctrine (full modern grid) — https://learnwardleymapping.com/doctrine/ (verified). Climatic patterns — https://wardleypedia.org/mediawiki/index.php/Climatic_patterns *(found via search; parent wiki verified)*. Gameplay — Chapter 5, https://medium.com/wardleymaps/the-play-and-a-decision-to-act-8eb796b1dff1 (verified as part of the chapter list).
resources.maintainer: Simon Wardley (originals); doctrine grid adapted by **Tasshin Fogleman** for Learn Wardley Mapping.
resources.started: Cheat sheet April 2016; doctrine post 16 August 2016.
resources.status: Wardley's originals are frozen (blog dormant since Feb 2024). The Learn Wardley Mapping doctrine grid is the actively maintained version. There is **no single canonical, actively maintained, openly licensed gameplay list** — this is a genuine gap in the ecosystem.
resources.licence: ⚠️ **Mixed — be careful.** Blog originals are **CC BY-SA 3.0**. Learn Wardley Mapping's doctrine grid is **CC BY-SA 4.0**. Book chapters are **CC BY-SA 4.0**. WardleyPedia's climatic patterns page has **no stated licence**.
resources.what_it_is: The reference furniture of the technique. The **cheat sheet** post defines the four constituent parts of any map — *anchor* (the user need), *position* (visibility, derived from the chain of needs), *types* (activities, practices, data, knowledge) and *evolution* (stages I–IV) — and stresses that evolution is measured by **ubiquity vs certainty**, explicitly *not* by time-based diffusion curves, which is the single most commonly misunderstood point in the whole method. It also gives weak signals for each stage. The **doctrine** post gives the canonical ten: focus on user need; use a common language; be transparent; challenge assumptions; remove duplication and bias; use appropriate methods; think small; think aptitude and attitude; design for constant evolution; enable purpose, autonomy and mastery — defined as *"basic universal principles applicable to all industries,"* distinct from context-specific gameplay and from climatic patterns. Learn Wardley Mapping's grid expands this to roughly **40 principles across four phases**: *Stop Self-Destructive Behaviour*, *Becoming More Context Aware*, *Better for Less*, *Continuously Evolving*.
resources.limitations: **There is no official doctrine poster** — I found no canonical printable artefact from Wardley himself. The two doctrine-assessment tools that existed (Chris Daniel's at doctrine.wardleymaps.com, and Justin Stach's Google-Forms-based Doctrine Grid Tool) are both listed as discontinued by Learn Wardley Mapping; doctrine.wardleymaps.com no longer resolves. The 10-item and 40-item doctrine lists coexist without a clear statement of which supersedes which, which confuses newcomers. Climatic patterns and gameplay have **no well-maintained standalone list** — the book chapters are the only reliable source, and they are long-form prose rather than reference tables. Blog images are low-resolution.
resources.attribution: Match the source precisely. Blog material: "Simon Wardley, *Bits or pieces?*, CC BY-SA 3.0." LWM doctrine grid: "Learn Wardley Mapping, adapted by Tasshin Fogleman from Simon Wardley's posts and *Better for Less*, CC BY-SA 4.0." Book material: CC BY-SA 4.0. **Do not merge these under one notice** — 3.0 and 4.0 are different licences.

resources.name: What do Wardley maps really map? A settler writes (critique)
resources.maintainer: **Matt Edgar**
resources.status: Live, stable. WordPress.com hosted.
resources.licence: **No explicit licence statement** — assume all rights reserved. Standard fair-dealing quotation only.
resources.what_it_is: The most substantive published critique of Wardley mapping, and the one that has genuinely stuck — a version of its central objection now appears in the Wikipedia article. Edgar, self-identifying as "a serial settler," raises three objections. First, that organising around pioneers/settlers/town planners is actively harmful, producing turf wars rather than clarity — he cites Orange Group wasting effort arguing about which category the app store belonged to. Second, that the evolution axis implies an inevitable left-to-right progression that reality does not honour: components stall, and components move backwards, and *"we're terrible at making predictions. Especially about the future."* Third and most damagingly, that **"Wardley maps are therefore an artefact of social science, not a life science"** — that the x-axis measures **level of consensus**, not objective evolution, which means the technique is manipulable and, rather than exposing assumptions for challenge, may **launder assumptions into facts and delegitimise challenge while still manufacturing consensus.**
resources.limitations: From 2017; does not engage with the doctrine grid or with anything from the last nine years of practice. Blog-length, not rigorous — it is an argument, not a study. No licence, so you can quote briefly but not reproduce.
resources.attribution: "Matt Edgar, *What do Wardley maps really map? A settler writes* (2017)." Short quotations with attribution under fair dealing; **no reproduction of the full post**, and no assumption of reuse rights.

resources.name: Where the map ends: understanding Wardley maps' limitations (critique)
resources.maintainer: **Danny Buerkli**
resources.status: Live on Medium.
resources.licence: Medium default — **all rights reserved** unless the author states otherwise. Fair-dealing quotation only.
resources.what_it_is: The most *useful* critique, precisely because it is not adversarial. Buerkli sets out four structural limitations and is explicit that these are inherent constraints reflecting the method's assumptions, not defects. **One:** maps show how components evolve from genesis to commodity but cannot tell you *which new components will emerge* in genesis — the map is blind to the thing that will disrupt it. **Two:** components only move along the evolution axis under competitive pressure; absent competition, they simply sit still, so the predictive machinery stops working in monopolies, regulated markets and internal-only landscapes. **Three:** a map can only represent what its creators already understand — *"you can't map what you don't see."* **Four:** usefulness depends entirely on choosing the right scope and resolution, and there are no codified rules for doing so — it takes experience the method does not teach. His closing move is the right one: the question is not whether Wardley mapping is flawed but whether it is more useful than the alternatives for a given problem.
resources.limitations: Medium-hosted with all-rights-reserved defaults. Short. It bounds the method without offering a remedy — pair it with Chris Daniel's *Where the Doctrine Ends* for the "so what do we do" half.
resources.attribution: "Danny Buerkli, *Where the map ends: understanding Wardley maps' limitations* (February 2025)." Brief quotation with attribution; no reproduction.

resources.name: Where the Doctrine Ends (critique)
resources.maintainer: **Chris Daniel**
resources.started: **2 June 2026** — the most recent substantive critique found.
resources.status: Live.
resources.licence: **CC BY-SA 4.0** (site-wide notice on wardleymaps.com). **This is the only major critique you can freely quote and adapt.**
resources.what_it_is: A qualified critique from inside the practice — Daniel calls it *"a divergence, not a dismissal."* His argument is that Wardley mapping excels at diagnosis and fails at driving action: *"Most organisations can read their landscape well enough. What stops them is rarely a missing map."* He identifies three problems. The **action gap** — doctrine diagnoses inertia but does not overcome it, and seeing a problem is categorically different from solving it. **Incentive blindness** — maps don't change budgets or how people vote, and organisations run two parallel strategies, the stated one and the one revealed by the budget. And **incompleteness** — doctrine *"teaches you to spot inertia on the map and plan around it"* but cannot *"get a leadership team to vote against its own incentives."* His proposal is not better mapping but attention to the machinery of inertia: how budgets are allocated and how decisions are actually made.
resources.limitations: One consultant's view, published on his own commercial site alongside his services. Newer and less tested than Edgar's critique. Offers a direction rather than a method.
resources.screenshot_target: https://www.wardleymaps.com/commentaries (the commentaries index, which shows the recency of the site)
resources.attribution: "Chris Daniel, *Where the Doctrine Ends*, WardleyMaps.com, CC BY-SA 4.0." **Freely quotable and adaptable**, ShareAlike applies to derivatives.

resources.name: Wardley mapping in security — Threat Models and Wardley Maps
resources.maintainer: **Brook S.E. Schoenfield, Dave van Stein, Dinis Cruz, Izar Tarandach, Jakub Kaluzny, Krzysztof Daniel** — Open Security Summit, Threat Modeling project
resources.started: **Open Security Summit 2022**, March mini-summit; 90-minute working session (18:00–19:30 Monday).
resources.status: Session page live; a video recording is stated to be on YouTube *(link unverified)*.
resources.licence: Open Security Summit terms; not stated on the session page. **Treat as unknown.**
resources.what_it_is: The single most credentialed gathering on Wardley mapping in security — Schoenfield, Tarandach and Cruz are established threat-modelling authorities, not mapping enthusiasts. The session explores *"the use of Wardley Maps in Security, and how Wardley Maps could be the missing piece of the puzzle when doing Threat Models."* The framing matters: the claim is not that maps replace threat models, but that threat modelling lacks a way to reason about *where the landscape is going*, and mapping supplies it. It is a working session rather than a lecture, so the recording is a genuine practitioner argument rather than a polished talk.
resources.limitations: From 2022. The recording link is stated but not verified — confirm before publishing. Working-session format means it is discursive and less immediately actionable than van Stein's written article. Licence unknown.
resources.attribution: "Threat Models and Wardley Maps, Open Security Summit 2022," crediting the six named presenters. Licence unknown — link, don't reproduce.

resources.name: Using Wardley Mapping for Optimizing Your Threat Modeling Strategy
resources.maintainer: **Dave van Stein**, Xebia
resources.status: Live and recently updated.
resources.licence: Xebia corporate blog; **all rights reserved.** Fair-dealing quotation only.
resources.what_it_is: The most concrete, most actionable security application I found, and the one to build a security page around. Van Stein's argument is that teams jump straight into STRIDE and drown in detail, and that a Wardley map should sit *above* the threat model as a targeting layer. The method: build a high-level map of the system positioning components by commoditisation with the responsible team marked for each layer; then apply Wardley's opportunity framework — validate assumptions at **team boundaries**, marked with triangles, because handoff points between teams are *"bias hotspots"*; assess organisational capability and expertise gaps that threaten secure implementation; and challenge the attack surface by asking which components could be **eliminated entirely** rather than defended. Only then run STRIDE, on the areas the map identified. He works a concrete example of an API system with DNS, WAF, proxies and load balancers, and includes four maps with annotated problem areas. His own framing: *"it hopefully will provide you more overview on where to apply STRIDE without getting lost in dirty details."*
resources.limitations: Vendor blog, all rights reserved, so nothing can be mirrored. One consultant's method, not a validated framework. Assumes STRIDE familiarity. The maps are illustrative rather than from a real engagement.
resources.attribution: "Dave van Stein, Xebia." **Do not reproduce the diagrams** — they are Xebia's copyright. Describe the method, link for the maps.

resources.name: Evolution-informed Security Architecture: Using Wardley Mapping (SABSA)
resources.url: https://sabsa.org/evolution-informed-security-architecture-wardley-maps/ (verified). ⚠️ A related SABSA page, https://sabsa.org/webinar-evolution-informed-security-architecture-using-wardley-mapping/, is **blocked by robots.txt** and could not be fetched.
resources.maintainer: **Mario Platt**, then Independent Consultant and Strategy Director at Practical DevSecOps; hosted by **The SABSA Institute** (webinar WB105).
resources.status: Abstract page live; **the recording is members-only.**
resources.licence: SABSA Institute; all rights reserved, members-only content.
resources.what_it_is: The most institutionally serious treatment of Wardley mapping in security architecture — SABSA is an established enterprise security architecture framework with a formal certification track, and this webinar maps Wardley's technique onto it. Platt introduces mapping as a strategy-development framework and then demonstrates *"how it can help inform decisions at different layers of the SABSA matrix,"* using climatic patterns and doctrine to help security architects spot risks and opportunities in enterprise security delivery. The significance is the direction of travel: rather than security people discovering mapping, this is an established security architecture body incorporating it.
resources.limitations: **The recording is behind SABSA membership** — you can cite the abstract but most readers cannot watch it. From 2020. A sibling SABSA URL is robots.txt-blocked, so verification is partial. Presupposes SABSA knowledge.
resources.attribution: "Mario Platt, *Evolution-informed Security Architecture: Using Wardley Mapping for Situational Awareness and Decision Making*, The SABSA Institute (WB105, May 2020)." Members-only content — link to the abstract only, never reproduce.

resources.name: The Value Flywheel Effect
resources.maintainer: **David Anderson, Mark McCann, Michael O'Reilly**; IT Revolution
resources.status: In print, all formats (paperback, eBook, audiobook) across major retailers.
resources.licence: Commercial; all rights reserved.
resources.what_it_is: The best-known applied Wardley mapping book and the one most likely to land with an engineering leadership audience. Subtitled *Power the Future and Accelerate Your Organization to the Modern Cloud*, it uses *"Wardley Mapping and other sense-making approaches"* to help organisations anticipate market changes and user needs, structured around a four-phase flywheel. David Anderson is explicitly described by the publisher as a member of the Wardley Mapping community, and **Simon Wardley wrote the foreword**, endorsing it for understanding competitive landscapes in the modern industrial era. It is the clearest evidence that mapping has escaped its originator and been productised into a repeatable organisational method.
resources.limitations: Commercial and closed — nothing quotable at length. Mapping is one technique among several; it is not a mapping textbook. Cloud/serverless framing dates it somewhat. From 2022.
resources.attribution: "David Anderson, Mark McCann and Michael O'Reilly, *The Value Flywheel Effect* (IT Revolution, 2022)." Cover image for review purposes only.
